title: Additions to the Entity List
summary:
The United States announced two notable moves: it tightened export controls by adding new companies and addresses to its watchlist, and it temporarily closed part of the Atlantic bluefin tuna commercial fishery for the rest of October and November.

On exports, the Department of Commerce added 26 companies and three addresses in China, Turkey, and the United Arab Emirates to the Entity List. Officials say these groups helped move American-made parts to Iran and its affiliates, including components found in weaponized drones used by militant groups. As a result, any shipment to these listed parties now needs a license, and most requests will likely be denied. The rule also extends to foreign firms majority-owned by a listed party. There is a short grace period for shipments that were already en route as of October 8, which must be completed by November 7.

On fisheries, federal managers closed the General category for Atlantic bluefin tuna through November 30, after quota monitoring showed catch levels had reached or were projected to reach their limits for this time period. During the closure, commercial vessels may not keep large bluefin tuna, though tag-and-release is allowed. The fishery is set to reopen on December 1.

Who benefits? National security officials and policymakers see the export steps as a way to slow the flow of sensitive electronics and aircraft parts into conflict zones, especially where they may end up in drones. Companies that follow the rules also gain clearer guidance on who they must avoid. On the water, closing the tuna fishery now supports conservation goals, helps keep the United States aligned with international quota commitments, and aims to maintain a sustainable fishery for future seasons.

Who is negatively affected? The newly listed companies, their majority-owned affiliates, and trading partners may face blocked deals, supply chain delays, and reputational costs. Some United States exporters will lose customers or face added compliance hurdles. The tuna closure will temporarily sideline commercial bluefin harvests, affecting fishermen, dealers, and coastal businesses tied to that catch, as well as buyers who rely on fresh supply during this period.
